<document>
# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

response:
I've read it. Here's my restatement, then my assessment.

## What the comment claims

Using the Halden microdata, Varga and Holm argue that four problems account for most of the reported 23.4% per-hour gain:

1. **Attrition.** Seven of the nine withdrawals happened *after* the reduced schedule began, not during preparation, and six of the nine cited workload or inability to maintain output.
2. **Output measure.** In the 23 organisations that submitted records, the manager index exceeded the record-based index by 3.8 points on average (98.9 vs 95.1), and was higher in 19 of 23 cases.
3. **Hours denominator.** In the 27 organisations with time tracking, actual hours fell 14.1%, not 20%. In the 17 with both records and time tracking, the per-hour gain is 10.8%.
4. **Revenue.** Against 4.1% inflation, the nominal +1.4% is about −2.6% in real terms.

They also argue:
- **Sectors.** "Sector-general" is an artefact of the per-hour metric.
- **Novelty.** The residual ~11% gain is plausibly novelty, because self-reported energy declined between months three and six.
- **Meetings.** Varden's meetings analysis is post hoc and should not be cited.

They conclude that per-hour gains from reduced-hours schemes are "entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty".

I checked the arithmetic in Table 2 and the revenue adjustment:
- 95.1 / 0.8 ≈ +18.9%
- 98.4 / 0.859 ≈ +14.6%
- 34.6 / 40.3 ≈ 0.859
- 95.4 / 86.1 ≈ +10.8%
- 1.014 / 1.041 ≈ 0.974, so about −2.6% real

These are all correct. One component figure doesn't reconcile (point 4 under "Problems" below).

## Overall verdict

Sections 1–5 are a strong, data-based correction and should be taken at full weight. The conclusion is a different matter. It goes well beyond the corrections, contradicts the comment's own residual estimate, and leaves out the strongest evidence on the question, which is the randomised trial it cites elsewhere. This document makes the opposite error to the Halden working paper: Halden overstated a provisional gain, and this comment declares a question settled in the negative when the evidence leaves it open.

## What the comment establishes

- **The attrition finding is the most important new fact.** It directly contradicts the working paper's description ("withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons"), and it comes from the microdata, not from inference. With six of nine withdrawals citing output problems, the 61 are survivors. The continuation rate is 56 of 70 (80%), and that is the figure Halden should report.
- **Manager inflation is systematic.** Nineteen of 23 managers reported higher output than their records showed. That is a consistent direction, not noise, and the authors' explanation (rounding toward success, not bad faith) is reasonable.
- **The actual-hours cut was about 14%, not 20%.** This closely matches Varden's 13% for case-processing, measured independently from timesheets. Two sources agreeing makes this close to settled for this kind of work.
- **Revenue and sector-generality.** Both corrections are right. The retail record-based figure (−11.2%) rests on only three organisations, but it agrees in direction with everything else.

## Problems

**1. The conclusion contradicts the comment's own estimate.** After the corrections the authors can make, a gain of 10.8% remains. They report no confidence interval for it, so they haven't shown it is consistent with zero. They don't even estimate how much attrition would reduce it. Calling a gain "entirely an artifact" while your own best estimate is +10.8% requires showing that novelty accounts for that remainder, and the comment doesn't show it.

**2. The novelty argument uses the wrong evidence and leaves out the right evidence.**
- **Energy is self-reported, not output.** A decline in energy doesn't show that output per hour declined.
- **The month-ten projection is a straight line through two points** (0.61 at month three, 0.29 at month six). It could just as well be levelling off.
- **The direct test was available and isn't reported.** Halden collected the output index *monthly*, and the authors have the microdata. If novelty drives the gain, record-based output per actual hour should decline from month one to month six in the 17 organisations with full data. That is the analysis that would test their claim, and they don't present it.
- **"The burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter" is not a substitute for that analysis.** "Six months can't distinguish novelty from a durable effect" is correct, and it is a reason to call the question *open*. Their own sentence supports "undetermined", not "artifact".

**3. The comment leaves out Varden's main registered result.** It cites Varden's counter stratum as "the most reliable finding in the literature". But the same trial's case-processing stratum found +12.5% output per actual hour (CI +6.9 to +18.4), and that stratum has:
- randomisation, so no selection;
- administrative output records, so no manager inflation;
- timesheet hours, so no denominator problem;
- nine months of follow-up, longer than Halden's six.

That result addresses three of the comment's four mechanisms directly, and its interval is narrower than the counter stratum's: 14 clusters against 10. Citing the trial's negative stratum as most reliable while ignoring its positive one is selective use of evidence.

The two estimates also converge: Halden corrected to +10.8%, and Varden case-processing measured +12.5%. They come from different designs, with different weaknesses, in different settings. That agreement is evidence the residual is real for backlog and knowledge work, at least over six to nine months. Novelty could affect both studies, since staff knew they were being evaluated, but the comment would need to engage with that agreement, not omit it.

**4. One hours figure doesn't reconcile.** The comment says actual hours rose by +0.7 hours per day on the four working days and by 1.6 hours on the day off. That implies roughly 4 × 8.7 + 1.6 ≈ 36.4 hours per week. The reported total is 34.6, which implies about 8.25 hours per working day. Either the +0.7 refers to a different subset or base, or one figure is wrong. The 14.1% total comes straight from the totals and is probably unaffected, but the decomposition needs correcting or explaining.

**5. The Table 2 rows use different samples.** The four specifications use 61, 23, 27 and 17 organisations, so the step-by-step reduction mixes changes of measure with changes of sample. A clean breakdown would compute all four specifications on the same 17 organisations, with intervals. The Data Note acknowledges the subsets differ, which is to the authors' credit, but the conclusion then treats the subset estimates as a general verdict.

**6. Section 7 misrepresents Varden and dismisses the meetings hypothesis too strongly.**
- **Varden did not "cite it as a mechanism".** Varden labelled the analysis unregistered and based on seven offices. It explicitly said a correlation of this kind "cannot establish a mechanism", and registered a confirmatory test. That is exactly how a light, post hoc hypothesis should be handled.
- **"Selected for analysis after the results were known" may not be accurate.** Varden says the calendar data were collected in month six at managers' request, before the nine-month results existed. When the analysis was decided is unclear from either document.
- **The right weight is light, not zero.** Saying the hypothesis "should not be cited" treats a hypothesis with a registered confirmatory test as if it were already refuted.
- **The meetings hypothesis is also the main alternative to novelty.** If per-hour gains come from removing low-value meetings, they are real and potentially durable, not artefacts. They may simply not require cutting hours. By dismissing it, the comment drops the explanation most likely to compete with its own.

**7. The scope of the conclusion is too broad.** The comment re-analyses one pilot. Its conclusion covers "the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes" in general. Even if the Halden residual were entirely novelty, that wouldn't extend to Varden, whose design rules out selection and measurement artefacts.

**Minor points:**
- CPI is a rough deflator for organisational revenue. Output-price deflators by sector would be better, though the direction of the correction is surely right.
- The conclusion calls the negative finding "best-supported" without mentioning that Varden's sick-day reduction (−29% against control) is also randomised and supports the other side of the overall picture.

## A calibrated version of the conclusion

> Using the Halden microdata, we find that the pilot's headline overstated the per-hour gain. Seven of nine withdrawals occurred after the schedule began, mostly for output reasons. Manager-reported output exceeded record-based output by about four points. Actual hours fell by about 14%, not 20%. In the 17 organisations where all corrections are possible, the gain in output per actual hour is about 11%. This is less than half the reported figure, before any adjustment for attrition, and applies to a non-random subset.
>
> This residual is close to the 12.5% found in Varden County's randomised case-processing stratum, which is free of the selection and measurement problems we identify. Whether such gains persist beyond six to nine months, or reflect novelty, is open. The monthly output data and Varden's 24-month follow-up can test it. In coverage-bound work, both the corrected pilot data and the Varden trial indicate that reduced hours reduce output per employee.

## Taking the three documents together

| Question | Status |
|---|---|
| Halden's 23.4% headline is inflated | **Settled.** About half of it comes from the hours denominator and manager reporting, and attrition inflates it further. |
| Actual hours fall by about 13–14%, not 20% | **Close to settled** for backlog and knowledge work. Two independent sources agree. |
| Coverage-bound work loses output per employee when coverage isn't restored | **Well supported.** The Varden RCT and the Halden retail and reversion pattern agree. |
| Sickness absence falls | **Well supported.** Randomised evidence (Varden −29%). |
| A real per-actual-hour gain of about 10–12% in backlog and knowledge work | **Supported over six to nine months** by two converging designs. |
| The gain persists beyond nine months | **Open.** Tests: the monthly Halden trajectory, Varden at 24 months. |
| The gain comes from removing meetings rather than from rest | **Open, light evidence.** Test: Varden's registered confirmatory analysis. |

I can draft a response letter to the journal, or set out the specific analyses (same-sample decomposition, monthly trajectory, attrition bounds) that would settle the open questions.
